newsitem.title: USA: Sears makes first hostile bid, for rest of Maxserv.
newsitem.headline: Sears makes first hostile bid, for rest of Maxserv.

text.p: Sears, Roebuck & Co. launched its first hostile takeover bid Tuesday, a week after talks to buy the rest of its majority-owned Maxserv Inc. customer service support operation broke down.
The nation's second-largest retailer launched a tender offer of $7 a share for the 35.6 precent of Maxserv it does not already own in a deal that would be worth about $27 million.
Sears said it would not raise the offer, though analysts said it may have to if wants to secure the rest of the company without a drawn-out fight.
Sears withdrew its friendly $7-a-share offer on Jan. 27 after a special committee of Maxserv's board voted to reject the bid. Maxserv said it remained willing to negotiate.
Sears first expressed interest in buying the rest of Maxserv, which has about 10.9 million shares outstanding, in early December.

The ties between Austin, Tex.-based Maxserv, which tracks customer service calls and replacement parts sales for products such as Sears appliances, and the retailer go back several years. Sears has about 2,300 stores nationwide.

"Sears sees an opportunity to grow this operation," said analyst David Tuong at Argus Research. "It would help Sears to respond to customers' service calls more promptly and register when a service call came in."
"It's an unusual situation," said Joel Krasner, an analyst who follows Maxserv for Southcoast Capital Corp., noting Sears accounts for about 90 percent of Maxserv's business.
"The stock is worth more than $7 a share and I'm advising my clients not to tender their shares," Krasner said. "I believe they'll ultimately agree at a higher price."
Sears spokesman Tom Nicholson said it was the company's first hostile tender offer. The two sides continue to talk but Sears does not want to raise its offer, he said.
"Since we already own (about) 64 percent of the stock, I believe that (the $7) offer will stand," Nicholson said.
But some investors were betting Sears would raise its bid, and drove Maxserv stock up 12.5 cents to $7.125 on Nasdaq.
"Sears has the pockets to pay whatever it wants to pay and at some point they'll reach the right price," said Tuong at Argus Research.
Neil Johnson, MaxServ senior vice president and chief financial officer, said the company expected to respond to Sears' offer later Tuesday.
Southcoast Capital's Krasner said a deal could be struck soon if the two sides can agree on price. He values Maxserv at $8 to $9 a share.
Joseph Ronning at Brown Brothers Harriman said he did not believe that the bid meant Sears was going to use hostile offers in future acquisitions.
"Sears wants to get the deal done, but they don't want to grossly overpay," he said. "Acquisitions are going to be the way of life for Sears but hostile takeovers will not be."
Sears stock added $1.125 to $48.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
